lessons.title: Synthesis — asking, and answering
lessons.gloss: synthesis — three verb families and two question words become a conversation

segments.text: Nothing new in this chapter. Say "I eat" and "I live." (Como. Vivo.)
Something quietly enormous happened over the last four chapters, and it is worth saying out loud before you use it.

Spanish has three verb families. You now hold the singular of all three. That is not three facts — it is a machine: hand it any regular verb you meet for the rest of your life, and you can already say what you do with it, what a friend does, and what somebody else does.
Two question words turn that machine outward. ¿Qué? asks what. ¿Dónde? asks where. With them, the forms stop being an exercise and start being a conversation.
— ¿Qué bebes? — Bebo café. ¿Y tú? — Yo también. ¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en Madrid.
Four lines, and every single word in them is something you built yourself. No new vocabulary was needed to get here — only the endings, one slot at a time.
Notice what the questions cost: nothing. You did not learn a question form. You put ¿qué? or ¿dónde? in front of a verb you already had.

segments.instruction: the exchange above, both parts, without stopping

segments.instruction: it again, swapping in comes for bebes
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it again, swapping in *comes* for *bebes*]

segments.text: Run it until the question and the answer arrive together.

segments.prompt: Ask a friend what they eat.

feedback.correct: Yes — the question word, then the tu form.
feedback.incorrect: Que comes. The question word goes in front of the form you already have.

segments.prompt: Ask a friend where they live.
How many verb families do you now hold in the singular?

feedback.correct: All three — and that covers every regular verb.

segments.text: How many verb families do you hold? (Three — and that is all of them.) What did the question words cost you? (Nothing — they sit in front of forms you already had.) Ask where somebody lives. (¿Dónde vives?)
